title: Job Answers: My Friends Are Like Dry Wadis
summary: Job replies to Eliphaz, saying his grief is heavier than the sand of the sea and that the arrows of the Almighty have poisoned his spirit. He wishes God would crush him and end his life, taking comfort only that he has not denied the words of the Holy One. He then turns to his friends, comparing them to desert streams that vanish when travelers need them, and challenges them to show him where he has gone wrong.
story: Eliphaz has just finished his speech in chapters 4 and 5, urging Job to accept God's discipline and promising restoration. Job's reply runs through chapters 6 and 7. In this chapter he defends his outburst in chapter 3, describes his pain, and turns on his friends for failing him. In chapter 7 he will address God directly. From here on, the dialogue grows more intense: the friends press their argument, and Job increasingly moves past them to seek an answer from God himself.
historical:
Job draws his images from the life of the desert and its trade routes. Tema was an oasis town in northwest Arabia, and Sheba was a kingdom in southern Arabia known for its trade in incense and spices. Caravans from both crossed the desert along routes marked by wells and seasonal streams. A caravan that counted on water and found none could perish in the wasteland.

The wadis Job describes are streambeds that flood with water after rain or snowmelt and then dry up completely in the heat of summer. They are common across the Middle East. In winter they can run high, dark with melting ice and snow from the hills; by the dry season they are empty channels of stone and sand.
cultural:
Job's complaint in verses 5-7 uses the language of food. A wild donkey doesn't bray when it has grass, and an ox doesn't low over its fodder; animals complain only when something is wrong. Tasteless food eaten without salt, or the white of an egg (the Hebrew phrase is uncertain, and some translations render it as the juice of a plant), stands for the flavorless comfort his friends have offered. His loud complaint, he says, is proof that something is truly wrong.

Friendship in the ancient world carried strong obligations of loyalty, expressed in the word chesed, steadfast kindness. A friend was expected to stand by someone in trouble. Job says that a despairing man should have the kindness of his friend even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty. The Hebrew of verse 14 is difficult, and translations differ: some read it as the BSB does, others take it to mean that the one who withholds kindness from a friend is the one who forsakes the fear of the Almighty. He also insists he never asked them for money, a bribe, or rescue from enemies; he only asked for their loyalty, and they failed him. Casting lots for an orphan and bartering a friend (verse 27) were images of the worst betrayal, treating the vulnerable as property.
literary: Job's speech moves in clear sections. He first describes the weight of his suffering (verses 1-7), then wishes for death (verses 8-13), then turns to his friends with the extended image of the deceitful wadis (verses 14-23), and finally challenges them directly (verses 24-30). The wadi image is one of the book's finest poetic passages, building the picture step by step: dark with ice, overflowing with snow, then vanishing in the heat, and caravans turning aside only to perish. The questions in verses 11-13 and 30 show Job's mind working rapidly between despair and defiance. Notice that Job's tone toward his friends is sharper than toward God in this chapter; his direct address to God comes in chapter 7.

outline.t: Job challenges his friends to show his wrong

doctrines.note: Job insists that his complaint is proportionate to his pain. The chapter shows that sufferers are entitled to speak of their suffering and that friends should listen before judging their words.
Even while wishing for death, Job clings to one comfort: he has not denied the words of the Holy One. His faith is battered but not abandoned.

Job's rebuke of his friends shows what a community of faith owes the suffering: loyal kindness, patience with rash words, and honest listening. The failure of the friends is a warning to every community of believers.

words.note: Chesed, kindness, loyal love, steadfast love. It is one of the most important words in the Old Testament, often used of God's covenant faithfulness. Job says a despairing man should receive chesed from his friend. The friends' failure is a failure of this loyal love.
Nachal, a wadi or seasonal stream. Job compares his friends to wadis that flood in winter but vanish in summer. The image captures friends who appear dependable but fail when they are most needed.

Shaddai, the Almighty. Job says the arrows of the Almighty have pierced him. He attributes his suffering to God directly; unlike the reader, he knows nothing of the accuser, and he does not try to explain God away.

Tsedeq, righteousness, rightness. Job says his righteousness is at stake. He is not claiming to be sinless, but he is insisting that he is in the right in this dispute, and that the friends' accusation is unjust.

christ: Job's friends fail him in his hour of need, like streams that dry up when travelers need water most. The Gospels record a similar abandonment of Jesus in his suffering: “Then everyone deserted Him and fled” (Mark 14:50). The connection is thematic, not a prediction. But where Job's friends failed, Jesus proved to be the faithful friend, who said, “Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). In Christ, God shows the chesed Job longed for from his friends, a loyal love that does not vanish in the heat of trouble.

hard.q: Is it wrong for Job to ask God to crush him and end his life?
hard.a: Job's wish for death in verses 8-10 is a cry of pain, not a plan. He asks God to end his life; he does not take matters into his own hands. Several biblical figures express similar wishes in extreme distress, including Moses (Numbers 11:15), Elijah (1 Kings 19:4), and Jonah (Jonah 4:3). The Bible records these prayers without endorsing them as right judgments, and God responds to each with care rather than condemnation. Job's words show that faith and despair can coexist, and that it is better to bring such thoughts to God than to hide them. Readers who find themselves sharing Job's longing should not carry it alone; talking to a trusted friend, a pastor, a doctor, or a crisis line is an act of courage, not weakness, and help is available right now.

questions: Job compares his friends to streams that dry up when needed. Have you ever been that kind of friend, or needed a friend who stayed?
Job says a despairing person should receive kindness even if they are losing their faith. How can you show loyal love to someone whose faith is shaken?
Job asks his friends to show him where he has gone wrong instead of assuming it. How can we speak honestly to a suffering person without accusing them?
